headline: Today in Tech & Research
narrative_html:
Today in Tech: Monitoring Models, Managing Data, and Mamba's Evolution

Let's talk about what actually matters in today's batch of papers and announcements.

Model Monitoring Without Ground Truth

First up, there's this "CBPE" method for estimating binary classifier performance without ground truth labels. This is a genuinely useful development.

The problem they're solving is real: you deploy a model, but you don't know if it's still performing well because you don't have immediate access to the true labels. Traditional monitoring requires these labels, creating an annoying latency or making monitoring impossible.

What's interesting is they're moving beyond just accuracy estimation (which others have tackled) to estimate any metric defined from the confusion matrix - precision, recall, F1, etc. The approach treats confusion matrix elements as random variables and uses calibrated confidence scores to estimate their distributions.

The key insight: if your model is well-calibrated (its confidence scores actually correspond to probabilities of correctness), you can leverage this to estimate performance metrics without seeing the actual labels. They're also providing confidence intervals on these estimates, which is crucial for practical applications.

Nao Labs: Data-Aware Code Editor

This YC startup is building what they're calling "Cursor for Data" - basically a specialized code editor for data work. The core idea is integrating the code editor directly with data warehouses and adding an AI copilot that actually understands your data schema.

What's potentially valuable here is the focus on data-specific workflows. Regular code-focused LLM tools like Cursor don't natively connect to data warehouses, so they're autocompleting SQL without knowing your actual schema. The Nao editor shows you code diffs alongside data diffs, so you can immediately see how your changes affect outputs.

I'm skeptical about their "fork of VS Code" approach rather than building extensions, but their integration of RAG with your data schema and codebase could be genuinely useful for data teams. The emphasis on data quality checks and lineage impact analysis addresses real pain points.

PRE-Mamba: State Space Models for Event Cameras

This paper represents an interesting application of state space models (the tech behind Mamba) to a very specific domain: cleaning up noise from event cameras in rainy conditions.

Event cameras are these specialized sensors that capture changes in brightness at extremely high temporal resolution rather than full frames. They're great for high-dynamic-range scenes but get noisy in rain.

The technical innovation here is their "4D event cloud representation" with dual temporal scales and a "Multi-Scale State Space Model" that captures rain dynamics across different temporal and spatial scales. The computational efficiency is impressive - they're getting strong performance with only 0.26M parameters, which is tiny by modern standards.

This is part of a broader trend of state space models being applied to specialized domains beyond general text modeling.

Elastic Reasoning: Scalable Chain of Thought

This paper addresses a practical problem with LLMs that use chain-of-thought reasoning: they can ramble on forever, consuming tokens and compute. When you have real-world constraints on inference time or token budgets, this becomes problematic.

Their solution, "Elastic Reasoning," explicitly separates reasoning into two phases - thinking and solution - with separate budgets. The clever part is their training approach, which teaches models to be robust to truncated thinking processes. They use a "budget-constrained rollout strategy" that trains the model to adapt when its thinking gets cut short.

What makes this particularly useful is that it generalizes to unseen budget constraints without additional training. And interestingly, they found that this approach produces more concise reasoning even in unconstrained settings - suggesting that forcing the model to be efficient actually improves its reasoning quality.

Vision in Llama.cpp

The extract is incomplete, but the headline tells us that vision capabilities are now available in llama.cpp, which is significant for local deployment of multimodal models. Llama.cpp has been crucial for running LLMs on consumer hardware, and adding vision capabilities expands what's possible without cloud dependencies.

ICon: Data Selection Through In-Context Contribution

This paper tackles the problem of selecting the most valuable data for instruction tuning LLMs. Traditional methods either use expensive gradient-based measures or rely on manually designed heuristics.

Their approach, "ICon," leverages in-context learning to measure sample contribution without computing gradients. The insight is that you can use the model's performance shifts under in-context learning as a proxy for how valuable a sample would be for fine-tuning.

The results are impressive: models trained on just 15% of ICon-selected data outperform models trained on complete datasets by 5.42 percentage points. This suggests there's a lot of low-value or even harmful data in standard instruction tuning datasets.

The analysis of what makes high-contribution samples is interesting too - they're diverse in task types and have appropriate difficulty levels, not just the hardest examples.

The Thalidomide Derivative Revlimid: Pricing Ethics

This ProPublica piece tells the story of a cancer drug called Revlimid, a derivative of thalidomide that has become one of the best-selling pharmaceutical products ever with over $100 billion in sales.

The shocking part is the pricing: nearly $1,000 per pill, while it costs just 25 cents to manufacture. The journalist, who has multiple myeloma and takes the drug, notes that a month's supply costs about the same as a new Nissan Versa.

This isn't just abstract price gouging - the article mentions patients forced into debt or stopping treatment entirely because of the cost. The price has been hiked 26 times since launch, and the full story involves regulatory failures and exploitation of patent laws.

PlaceIt3D: Placing Objects in 3D Scenes

This paper introduces a new task for 3D scene understanding: placing objects in real 3D scenes based on natural language instructions. Given a 3D scene point cloud, a 3D asset, and a text prompt (like "put the chair next to the sofa"), the model needs to find valid placements.

What makes this challenging is that it's ambiguous (multiple valid solutions exist) and requires reasoning about 3D geometric relationships and available space. The authors have created a benchmark, evaluation protocol, and a dataset for training 3D LLMs on this task.

This is part of the broader trend toward more sophisticated 3D understanding in AI systems, which will be crucial for robotics and AR/VR applications.

item.title: Performance Estimation in Binary Classification Using Calibrated Confidence
item.summary:
Model monitoring is a critical component of the machine learning lifecycle,
safeguarding against undetected drops in the model's performance after
deployment. Traditionally, performance monitoring has required access to ground
truth labels, which are not always readily available. This can result in
unacceptable latency or render performance monitoring altogether impossible.
Recently, methods designed to estimate the accuracy of classifier models
without access to labels have shown promising results. However, there are
various other metrics that might be more suitable for assessing model
performance in many cases. Until now, none of these important metrics has
received similar interest from the scientific community. In this work, we
address this gap by presenting CBPE, a novel method that can estimate any
binary classification metric defined using the confusion matrix. In particular,
we choose four metrics from this large family: accuracy, precision, recall, and
F$_1$, to demonstrate our method. CBPE treats the elements of the confusion
matrix as random variables and leverages calibrated confidence scores of the
model to estimate their distributions. The desired metric is then also treated
as a random variable, whose full probability distribution can be derived from
the estimated confusion matrix. CBPE is shown to produce estimates that come
with strong theoretical guarantees and valid confidence intervals.

items.why:
Given your background—deep technical chops, strong interest in LLMs and tooling, a product/indie dev mindset, and a focus on practical, high-leverage ideas—this paper is **potentially worthwhile**, but probably not a must-read unless you have a direct need for robust model monitoring in your projects.

**Why it might be relevant:**  
The core contribution—estimating *any* confusion-matrix-based metric (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, etc.) for a deployed binary classifier *without labels*—is a step beyond typical label-free accuracy estimation. If you’re building or deploying ML-powered products (including LLM-based classifiers or agents), and especially if you want to offer monitoring/observability as a feature, this is a practical advance. The approach (using calibrated confidence to derive distributions over confusion matrix entries and thus any metric, with confidence intervals) is conceptually clean and could be valuable if you’re thinking about SaaS ML monitoring, compliance, or reliability tooling.

**Why you might skip or skim:**  
If your current or near-term work is more focused on LLM orchestration, agent systems, or non-classification tasks, the direct applicability is limited. The paper is more “incremental improvement in ML monitoring” than “paradigm shift.” It’s not a big, splashy new direction in LLMs, nor is it likely to set Twitter/HN on fire. But it *is* the kind of thing that could fly under the radar and be a hidden gem for the right product (e.g., if you want to build a next-gen ML monitoring tool or add robust monitoring to your LLM workflows).

**Bottom line:**  
If you’re actively considering building or improving ML/LLM monitoring tools, or want to keep a finger on the pulse of practical, under-discussed advances in model reliability, it’s worth a focused skim (especially the method and results sections). Otherwise, it’s safe to file under “good to know exists, but not urgent.”
items.overview:
Performance Estimation in Binary Classification Using Calibrated Confidence addresses a key challenge in machine learning model monitoring: assessing deployed model performance in the absence of ground truth labels. Traditional monitoring approaches depend on access to labeled data, which is often unavailable or delayed, leading to latency or making performance monitoring infeasible. Recent developments have enabled label-free estimation of model accuracy, but other important metrics derived from the confusion matrix—such as precision, recall, and F$_1$ score—have not been similarly addressed. This work introduces CBPE, a method that estimates any binary classification metric defined via the confusion matrix without requiring labels. CBPE operates by treating the confusion matrix elements as random variables, leveraging the model’s calibrated confidence scores to estimate their distributions. From these, it derives the full probability distribution of the desired metric, providing not only point estimates but also valid confidence intervals, supported by theoretical guarantees.

The practical significance of CBPE lies in its ability to provide robust, label-free estimates for a broad set of performance metrics in deployed binary classifiers. This is particularly relevant for scenarios where immediate access to ground truth is not possible, yet reliable monitoring is necessary for compliance, reliability, or product quality. The method’s reliance on calibrated confidence scores allows it to generalize beyond accuracy estimation, enabling monitoring of precision, recall, and F$_1$—metrics that may be more aligned with specific business or compliance requirements. The provision of confidence intervals for these estimates adds an additional layer of reliability, supporting more informed decision-making in production environments.

For practitioners focused on building or maintaining machine learning-powered products—especially those involving binary classification or offering monitoring and observability features—CBPE represents a practical advance. It is particularly applicable for those developing SaaS ML monitoring solutions or seeking to enhance the reliability of deployed models without access to labels. However, its direct applicability may be limited for work centered on LLM orchestration, agent systems, or tasks outside binary classification. The method is best regarded as an incremental but robust improvement in the domain of model monitoring, offering a concrete tool for scenarios where traditional label-dependent monitoring is impractical.
items.context: In binary classification, a model predicts one of two possible classes (e.g., spam vs. not spam), and its performance is typically measured using metrics derived from the confusion matrix, such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. These metrics usually require ground-truth labels to compute, but in many real-world deployments, especially in production or SaaS settings, true labels for new data may not be immediately available. This paper introduces a method to estimate any confusion-matrix-based metric for a deployed binary classifier without needing labels, by leveraging the model's calibrated confidence scores (i.e., probabilities that reflect the true likelihood of correctness). By modeling the distribution of these confidence scores, the approach can estimate not just point values but also confidence intervals for performance metrics, enabling robust monitoring and observability of ML systems in production, even when labels are scarce or delayed.

item.title: Launch HN: Nao Labs (YC X25) – Cursor for Data
item.summary:
Hey HN, we’re Claire and Christophe from nao Labs (https://getnao.io/). We just launched nao, an AI code editor to work with data: a local editor, directly connected with your data warehouse, and powered by an AI copilot with built-in context of your data schema and data-specific tools.

See our demo here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QmG6X-5ftZU

Writing code with LLMs is the new normal in software engineering. But not when it comes to manipulating data. Tools like Cursor don’t interact natively with data warehouses — they autocomplete SQL blindly, not knowing your data schema. Most of us are still juggling multiple tools: writing code in Cursor, checking results in the warehouse console, troubleshooting with an observability tool, and verifying in BI tool no dashboard broke.

When you want to write code on data with LLMs, you don’t care much about the code, you care about the data output. You need a tool that helps you write code relevant for your data, lets you visualize its impact on the output, and quality check it for you.

Christophe and I have each spent 10 years in data — Christophe was a data engineer and has built data platforms for dozens of orgs, I was head of data and helped data teams building their analytics & data products. We’ve seen how the business asks you to ship data fast, while you’re here wondering if this small line of code will mistakenly multiply the revenue on your CEO dashboard by x5. Which leaves you 2 choices: test extensively and ship slow. Not test and ship fast. That’s why we wanted to create nao: a tool really adapted to our data work, that would allow data teams to ship at business pace.

nao is a fork of VS Code, with built-in connectors for BigQuery, Snowflake, and Postgres. We built our own AI copilot and tab system, gave them a RAG of your data warehouse schemas and of your codebase. We added a set of agent tools to query data, compare data, understand data tools like dbt, assess the downstream impact of code in your whole data lineage.

The AI tab and the AI agent write straight away code matching your schema, may it be for SQL, python, yaml. It shows you code diffs and data diffs side by side, to visualize what your change did to the data output. And you can leave the data quality checks to the agent: detect missing or duplicated values, outliers, anticipate breaking changes downstream or compare dev and production data differences.

Data teams usually use nao for writing SQL pipelines, often with dbt. It helps them create data models, document them, test them, while making sure they’re not breaking data lineage and figures in the BI. In run mode, they also use it to run some analytics, and identify data quality bugs in production. For less technical profiles, it’s also a great help to strengthen their code best practices. For large teams, it ensures that the code & metrics remain well factorized and consistent.

Software engineers use nao for the database exploration part: write SQL queries with nao tab, explore data schema with the agent, and write DDL.

Question we often get is: why not just use Cursor and MCPs? Cursor has to trigger many MCP calls to get full context of the data, while nao has it always available in one RAG. MCPs stay in a very enclosed part of Cursor: they don’t bring data context to the tab. And they don’t make the UI more adapted to data workflows. Besides, nao comes as pre-packaged for data teams: they don’t have to set up extensions, install and authenticate in MCPs, build CI/CD pipelines. Which means even non-technical data teams can have a great developer experience.

Our long-term goal is to become the best place to work with data. We want to fine-tune our own models for SQL, Python and YAML to give the most relevant code suggestions for data. We want to enlarge our comprehension of all data stack tools, to become the only agnostic editor for any of your data workflow.

You can try it here: https://sunshine.getnao.io/releases/ - download nao, sign up for free and start using it. Just for HN Launch, you can create a temporary account with a simple username if you’d prefer not to use your email. For now, we only have Mac version but Linux and Windows are coming.

We’d love to hear your feedback — and get your thoughts on how we can improve even further the data dev experience!

items.why:
Given your background—deep in both systems design and LLM tooling, with a strong interest in human factors and productization—I think the Nao Labs HN post is worth at least a quick, focused read. The product is essentially "Cursor for Data": a VS Code fork with deep, native integration into data warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Postgres), and an LLM copilot with schema/contextual awareness, data lineage, and data quality tools. This is a clear step beyond generic code assistants, targeting the pain points of data engineering and analytics workflows, and aiming for a more seamless, context-rich experience for both technical and less technical users.

For you, the most interesting angles are probably:  
1. **Verticalization of LLM tooling**—Nao is a strong example of how LLMs can be made dramatically more useful when deeply embedded in domain-specific workflows and given access to rich, structured context (schemas, lineage, codebase, etc).  
2. **Productization and UX**—They’re not just bolting on an LLM, but rethinking the editor and workflow for data teams, including observability, diffs, and quality checks. This resonates with your own approach to maximizing expressiveness and ergonomics in tooling.  
3. **Market/Business Insight**—Their pitch and differentiation from Cursor/MCPs is instructive if you’re thinking about commercializing your own LLM tooling: they focus on out-of-the-box value, minimal setup, and targeting both technical and semi-technical personas.

It’s not a “fundamental” LLM breakthrough, but it’s a solid, well-executed example of the direction the LLM tooling ecosystem is heading—vertical, context-rich, and workflow-native. If you’re looking for inspiration or competitive signals for your own product ideas, it’s worth your time to skim the post and maybe watch the demo.
items.overview:
Nao Labs has introduced "nao," an AI-powered code editor specifically designed for working with data. Built as a fork of VS Code, nao offers native integrations with major data warehouses such as BigQuery, Snowflake, and Postgres. Its distinguishing feature is an AI copilot that possesses built-in awareness of the user's data schema, codebase, and data lineage. This enables the editor to generate code—across SQL, Python, and YAML—that is directly relevant to the user's data structures. The system also provides tools for querying and comparing data, understanding dbt workflows, assessing downstream impacts in data pipelines, and performing data quality checks such as identifying missing or duplicated values, outliers, and differences between development and production environments.

The product addresses several workflow challenges that data engineers and analysts commonly face. Traditional code editors and LLM-based autocompletion tools, like Cursor, lack native integration with data warehouses and do not maintain persistent context about data schemas or lineage. This forces users to switch between multiple tools for code writing, data validation, observability, and BI dashboard verification. Nao aims to consolidate these steps by providing a context-rich environment where users can write, test, and validate data code in one place. The editor supports side-by-side visualization of code and data diffs, facilitates the creation and documentation of data models (often with dbt), and helps maintain consistency and best practices across large teams. It is also positioned to be accessible to less technical users, streamlining setup and reducing the need for manual configuration or additional extensions.

From a systems design and productization perspective, nao exemplifies the trend of verticalizing LLM tooling—embedding language models deeply within domain-specific workflows and leveraging structured context to enhance utility. Its approach to product experience includes out-of-the-box value, minimal setup, and features tailored to both technical and semi-technical users. The team's differentiation from existing solutions like Cursor and MCPs is based on persistent schema awareness, integrated data workflow tools, and a user interface adapted for data-centric tasks. Nao is currently available for Mac, with Linux and Windows versions in development, and can be tried via a temporary account without email registration. The long-term goal is to support a wider range of data stack tools and to fine-tune their own models for more relevant code suggestions in SQL, Python, and YAML.
items.context: Nao Labs is a startup that has created a specialized code editor for data work by forking VS Code and deeply integrating it with popular data warehouses like BigQuery, Snowflake, and Postgres. Unlike generic AI code assistants, their tool embeds a large language model (LLM) that is aware of the specific database schemas, data lineage (how data flows and transforms through systems), and data quality metrics, allowing it to provide more relevant and accurate help for data engineering and analytics tasks. This approach exemplifies the 'verticalization' of LLM tooling—embedding AI deeply into a specific domain and workflow, rather than offering a one-size-fits-all solution. The product also emphasizes user experience by including features like observability (monitoring and understanding system behavior), diffs (comparing changes), and quality checks, aiming to make data work more accessible and efficient for both technical and less technical users. Their business strategy focuses on delivering immediate value with minimal setup, differentiating from more generic code assistants by targeting the unique needs of data teams.

item.title: PRE-Mamba: A 4D State Space Model for Ultra-High-Frequent Event Camera Deraining
item.summary:
Event cameras excel in high temporal resolution and dynamic range but suffer
from dense noise in rainy conditions. Existing event deraining methods face
trade-offs between temporal precision, deraining effectiveness, and
computational efficiency. In this paper, we propose PRE-Mamba, a novel
point-based event camera deraining framework that fully exploits the
spatiotemporal characteristics of raw event and rain. Our framework introduces
a 4D event cloud representation that integrates dual temporal scales to
preserve high temporal precision, a Spatio-Temporal Decoupling and Fusion
module (STDF) that enhances deraining capability by enabling shallow decoupling
and interaction of temporal and spatial information, and a Multi-Scale State
Space Model (MS3M) that captures deeper rain dynamics across dual-temporal and
multi-spatial scales with linear computational complexity. Enhanced by
frequency-domain regularization, PRE-Mamba achieves superior performance (0.95
SR, 0.91 NR, and 0.4s/M events) with only 0.26M parameters on EventRain-27K, a
comprehensive dataset with labeled synthetic and real-world sequences.
Moreover, our method generalizes well across varying rain intensities,
viewpoints, and even snowy conditions.

items.why:
Given your background—deep technical chops, strong interest in LLMs and tooling, and a focus on building products that leverage new tech—the PRE-Mamba paper is probably not a direct fit for your current goals. The work is highly specialized, focusing on event camera data (a niche but growing sensor modality) and the specific problem of "deraining" (removing rain noise) from that data using a novel 4D state space model. The technical contributions are impressive in their domain: efficient, high-precision processing with interesting architectural ideas (e.g., dual temporal scales, spatio-temporal decoupling, multi-scale state space modeling). But unless you’re actively working with event cameras, robotics, or computer vision for sensor data in adverse conditions, the practical overlap with your LLM-centric and product-focused interests is limited.

That said, there are a couple of "meta" reasons you might want to skim it. First, the architectural ideas—especially the use of state space models for efficient sequence processing—are part of a broader trend in deep learning (see: Mamba, S4, etc.) that's relevant to LLMs and sequence modeling in general. If PRE-Mamba introduces a novel way to handle high-frequency, high-dimensional sequential data efficiently, there could be patterns or abstractions worth borrowing for your own LLM workflow tools, especially if you ever want to process or visualize high-throughput event streams. Second, this paper is an example of how specialized, high-performance models are being built for new sensor modalities, which sometimes foreshadows broader shifts in ML tooling or product opportunities (think: the rise of vision transformers after success in niche CV tasks).

In summary: if your time is limited and you’re looking for research that will directly inform your LLM product work or business strategy, this paper is probably not the highest-leverage read. But if you’re curious about state space models or want to keep an eye on cross-pollination opportunities between sequence modeling in vision and NLP, a quick skim of the methods section could be worthwhile. Otherwise, you’re safe to skip it unless you’re specifically interested in event-based vision or want to spot early signals in that space.
items.overview:
PRE-Mamba is a point-based deraining framework designed for event cameras, which are sensors known for their high temporal resolution and dynamic range but are susceptible to dense noise in rainy conditions. The framework introduces a 4D event cloud representation that integrates dual temporal scales, enabling the preservation of high temporal precision while processing raw event data and rain artifacts. Central to the architecture is the Spatio-Temporal Decoupling and Fusion module (STDF), which facilitates shallow decoupling and interaction between temporal and spatial information, thereby enhancing the model's deraining capability. Additionally, PRE-Mamba incorporates a Multi-Scale State Space Model (MS3M) that captures rain dynamics across both dual-temporal and multi-spatial scales, achieving this with linear computational complexity. The system is further refined with frequency-domain regularization.

On the EventRain-27K dataset, which includes both synthetic and real-world labeled sequences, PRE-Mamba demonstrates strong empirical performance: it achieves a 0.95 Signal-to-Rain ratio (SR), a 0.91 Noise Reduction (NR) score, and processes at a rate of 0.4 seconds per million events, all with a compact model size of 0.26 million parameters. The method also generalizes across a range of rain intensities, different viewpoints, and even snowy conditions, highlighting its robustness in diverse adverse weather scenarios.

While PRE-Mamba's contributions are specialized to the domain of event-based vision and adverse weather mitigation, its architectural approaches—such as the use of state space models for efficient high-frequency, high-dimensional sequence processing—reflect broader trends in deep learning. These include the adoption of models like Mamba and S4 in sequence modeling. For those focused on large language models or general ML tooling, the relevance is primarily in potential cross-domain architectural insights, particularly regarding efficient sequence processing and multi-scale modeling. However, unless one is working directly with event cameras, robotics, or sensor data in challenging environments, the direct practical overlap with mainstream LLM development or productization is limited. Nonetheless, the paper may be of interest as an example of how specialized, high-performance models are being developed for emerging sensor modalities, which can sometimes signal future shifts in machine learning tooling and applications.
items.context: Event cameras are a type of sensor that, unlike traditional cameras which capture full images at fixed intervals, record changes in brightness at each pixel asynchronously and at extremely high temporal resolution, producing a stream of 'events' rather than frames. This makes them well-suited for capturing fast motion or operating in challenging conditions, but also introduces unique noise patterns, such as those caused by rain ('deraining' refers to removing this rain-induced noise). The PRE-Mamba paper proposes a novel deep learning architecture—a 4D state space model—that efficiently processes these high-frequency, high-dimensional event streams to clean up rain noise. State space models, recently popularized in deep learning (e.g., Mamba, S4), are designed for efficient sequence modeling and have shown promise as alternatives to transformers for handling long or complex sequences. While the application here is specialized (event camera deraining), the underlying architectural ideas—like multi-scale modeling and spatio-temporal decoupling—are part of a broader trend in sequence modeling that could have implications for other domains, including NLP and LLM tooling.

item.title: Scalable Chain of Thoughts via Elastic Reasoning
item.summary:
Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex
tasks by generating extended chains of thought (CoT). However, their
uncontrolled output lengths pose significant challenges for real-world
deployment, where inference-time budgets on tokens, latency, or compute are
strictly constrained. We propose Elastic Reasoning, a novel framework for
scalable chain of thoughts that explicitly separates reasoning into two
phases--thinking and solution--with independently allocated budgets. At test
time, Elastic Reasoning prioritize that completeness of solution segments,
significantly improving reliability under tight resource constraints. To train
models that are robust to truncated thinking, we introduce a lightweight
budget-constrained rollout strategy, integrated into GRPO, which teaches the
model to reason adaptively when the thinking process is cut short and
generalizes effectively to unseen budget constraints without additional
training. Empirical results on mathematical (AIME, MATH500) and programming
(LiveCodeBench, Codeforces) benchmarks demonstrate that Elastic Reasoning
performs robustly under strict budget constraints, while incurring
significantly lower training cost than baseline methods. Remarkably, our
approach also produces more concise and efficient reasoning even in
unconstrained settings. Elastic Reasoning offers a principled and practical
solution to the pressing challenge of controllable reasoning at scale.

items.why:
Absolutely, given your background and interests, I think "Scalable Chain of Thoughts via Elastic Reasoning" is worth at least a focused skim, possibly a deeper read. The core idea—explicitly separating "thinking" and "solution" phases in LLM reasoning, with independent resource budgets—directly addresses a real pain point in deploying LLMs for practical applications: unpredictable and often excessive token usage (and thus latency/cost). If you’re building LLM-backed products, especially ones that need to operate under real-world constraints (API limits, latency SLAs, user experience), this is a genuinely relevant innovation. Their approach to making models robust to truncated reasoning (via budget-constrained rollouts) is both clever and practical, and could inform your own system designs, especially if you want to offer users or customers guarantees around speed or cost.

From a product and tooling perspective, this paper is also interesting because it suggests a new interface paradigm for LLM reasoning: one where you can explicitly allocate and control resources for different phases of a task. That could translate into new user-facing controls, or backend features for your LLM combinator library or dashboard—e.g., letting users tune for "fast but maybe less thorough" vs. "take your time and maximize accuracy," or even visualize where budgets are being spent in a reasoning chain. This aligns with your ergonomic, maximally expressive system design philosophy, and could be a differentiator in the LLM tooling space.

Finally, while this paper is not (yet) a "big deal" in the sense of being widely discussed outside research circles, it’s exactly the kind of work that *should* be a big deal for practitioners building real products with LLMs. It’s also the kind of advance that, if you internalize it early, could give you a head start in building more robust, cost-effective, and user-friendly LLM-powered tools. So: if you’re looking for research that’s actionable and likely to shape the next wave of LLM product engineering, this is a good use of your time.
items.overview:
"Scalable Chain of Thoughts via Elastic Reasoning" addresses a central challenge in deploying large reasoning models (LRMs) for complex tasks: their tendency to produce uncontrolled and often excessive output lengths, which complicates real-world use where inference-time resources—such as token budgets, latency, or computational cost—are tightly limited. The proposed solution, Elastic Reasoning, introduces a novel framework that explicitly divides the reasoning process into two distinct phases: "thinking" and "solution." Each phase is allocated its own independent resource budget, allowing for fine-grained control over how much computational effort is spent on exploratory reasoning versus final answer generation. At inference time, the framework prioritizes the completeness of the solution segment, which increases the reliability of results when operating under strict resource constraints.

To ensure that models remain robust even when the "thinking" phase is truncated due to budget limitations, the authors present a lightweight budget-constrained rollout strategy, integrated into the GRPO training process. This approach teaches the model to adapt its reasoning process when cut short, and enables it to generalize to previously unseen budget constraints without the need for additional retraining. Empirical evaluations on mathematical benchmarks (AIME, MATH500) and programming benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, Codeforces) demonstrate that Elastic Reasoning maintains strong performance under tight resource budgets, while also reducing training costs compared to baseline methods. Additionally, the method yields more concise and efficient reasoning outputs even when resource constraints are relaxed.

From a practical perspective, Elastic Reasoning enables new possibilities for product and tooling design in LLM-backed systems. By allowing explicit allocation and control of resources for different reasoning phases, it supports the development of interfaces where users or system designers can tune trade-offs between speed, cost, and thoroughness. This could manifest as user-facing controls or backend features—such as adjusting for "fast but less thorough" versus "maximally accurate" reasoning, or visualizing resource expenditure within reasoning chains. The framework's emphasis on controllable, scalable reasoning is particularly relevant for applications that must adhere to API limits, latency service-level agreements, or predictable user experience requirements, and provides actionable strategies for building more robust and cost-effective LLM-powered tools.
items.context: Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 solve problems by generating sequences of text, often using a 'chain of thought'—a step-by-step reasoning process. However, in real-world applications, this can lead to unpredictable and sometimes excessive token usage, which directly impacts latency, cost, and user experience due to API limits or service-level agreements (SLAs). The paper 'Scalable Chain of Thoughts via Elastic Reasoning' introduces a method that explicitly separates the 'thinking' (reasoning) and 'solution' (final answer) phases in LLM workflows, allowing developers to independently allocate computational resources (like token budgets) to each phase. This makes it possible to control and optimize for speed, cost, or accuracy, and to build systems that are robust even if the reasoning process is cut short due to budget constraints. item.title: ICon: In-Context Contribution for Automatic Data Selection
item.summary:
Data selection for instruction tuning is essential for improving the
performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) and reducing training cost.
However, existing automated selection methods either depend on computationally
expensive gradient-based measures or manually designed heuristics, which may
fail to fully exploit the intrinsic attributes of data. In this paper, we
propose In-context Learning for Contribution Measurement (ICon), a novel
gradient-free method that takes advantage of the implicit fine-tuning nature of
in-context learning (ICL) to measure sample contribution without gradient
computation or manual indicators engineering. ICon offers a computationally
efficient alternative to gradient-based methods and reduces human inductive
bias inherent in heuristic-based approaches. ICon comprises three components
and identifies high-contribution data by assessing performance shifts under
implicit learning through ICL. Extensive experiments on three LLMs across 12
benchmarks and 5 pairwise evaluation sets demonstrate the effectiveness of
ICon. Remarkably, on LLaMA3.1-8B, models trained on 15% of ICon-selected data
outperform full datasets by 5.42% points and exceed the best performance of
widely used selection methods by 2.06% points. We further analyze
high-contribution samples selected by ICon, which show both diverse tasks and
appropriate difficulty levels, rather than just the hardest ones.

items.overview:
The paper introduces ICon (In-context Learning for Contribution Measurement), a new method for automatic data selection in the context of instruction tuning for Large Language Models (LLMs). Traditional approaches to data selection either rely on gradient-based measures, which are computationally expensive, or on manually crafted heuristics, which may not fully leverage the intrinsic qualities of the data and can introduce human bias. ICon addresses these limitations by using a gradient-free approach that leverages the implicit fine-tuning dynamics of in-context learning (ICL) to assess the contribution of individual data samples. The method comprises three components and operates by measuring performance shifts when data samples are presented in an ICL setting, thereby identifying high-contribution data without the need for gradient computation or manual indicator engineering.

Extensive experiments were conducted using ICon on three different LLMs, spanning 12 benchmarks and 5 pairwise evaluation sets. The results demonstrate that ICon is effective at identifying valuable data for instruction tuning. Notably, on the LLaMA3.1-8B model, training with only 15% of the data selected by ICon led to performance that exceeded models trained on the full dataset by 5.42 percentage points, and outperformed the best results from widely used selection methods by 2.06 percentage points. Further analysis of the samples chosen by ICon revealed that they encompass a diverse range of tasks and maintain an appropriate level of difficulty, rather than simply selecting the most challenging examples.

This work is particularly relevant for practitioners focused on LLM tooling and infrastructure, as efficient and automated data curation is increasingly recognized as a critical factor in LLM performance and cost-effectiveness. The gradient-free, plug-and-play nature of ICon suggests that it could be directly integrated into existing workflows for constructing, filtering, or augmenting datasets used in fine-tuning or evaluation. Even if not adopted in its entirety, the underlying principle of using ICL as a proxy for sample value—thereby avoiding both gradient computation and manual heuristics—may inform future approaches to data selection and inspire new tooling, especially in contexts where composability and observability are priorities. As data selection becomes a central concern in LLM development, methods such as ICon may play a foundational role in shaping best practices for both research and product applications.
items.context: Instruction tuning is a process where large language models (LLMs) are further trained on curated datasets of instructions and responses to improve their ability to follow user prompts. A key challenge in this process is data selection—choosing which examples to include for optimal model performance. Traditional methods often rely on heuristics or computationally expensive techniques like gradient-based influence estimation to assess the value of each data point. The ICon paper introduces a novel, gradient-free approach for automatic data selection by measuring each example's 'in-context contribution' (ICC): it evaluates how much a data point helps the model perform better on similar tasks when included as an in-context example (i.e., as part of the prompt, not the model weights). This method leverages in-context learning (ICL)—the ability of LLMs to generalize from examples provided in the prompt—to estimate data value efficiently, without retraining or backpropagation. For engineers building LLM systems, such a plug-and-play, automatic data selection technique could streamline dataset curation for instruction tuning, potentially leading to better models with less manual effort.

item.title: The Price of Remission
item.summary: ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published. The pain jolted me awake. It was barely dawn, a misty February morning in 2023. My side felt as if I’d been stabbed. I had been dealing with pain for weeks — a bothersome ache that felt like a bad runner’s cramp. But now it was so intense I had to brace myself against the wall to stand up. A few hours after arriving at the emergency room, I heard my name. A doctor asked me to follow him to a private area, where he told me a scan had uncovered something “concerning.” There were lesions, areas of bone destruction, on top of both of my hip bones and on my sternum. These were hallmarks of multiple myeloma. “Cancer,” he said. Multiple myeloma is a blood cancer that ravages bone, leaving distinctive holes in its wake. Subsequent scans showed “innumerable lesions” from my neck to my feet as well as two broken ribs and a compression fracture in my spine. There is no cure. I walked out of the ER in search of fresh air. I sat on a metal bench and did what many patients do. I turned to Google. The first link was a medical review stating that the average lifespan of a newly diagnosed patient was three to five years. My stomach churned. I soon learned that information was outdated. Most patients today live much longer, in large part due to a drug with a horrific past. It was a doctor at the hospital who first told me I would likely take a thalidomide drug as part of my treatment. That couldn’t be possible, I told him. I knew the story of thalidomide, or at least I thought I did. It represented one of the darkest chapters in the history of modern medicine, having caused thousands of severe birth defects after it was given to pregnant women in the 1950s and 1960s. The drug was banned in most of the world, and the scandal gave rise to the modern-day U.S. Food and Drug Administration. It turns out the drug once relegated to a pharmaceutical graveyard had new life as a cancer fighter. That drug I take is called Revlimid. It is a derivative of thalidomide, a slightly tweaked version of the parent compound. Revlimid is now one of the bestselling pharmaceutical products of all time, with total sales of more than $100 billion. It has extended tens of thousands of lives — including my own. But Revlimid is also, I soon learned, extraordinarily expensive, costing nearly $1,000 for each daily pill. (Although, I later discovered, a capsule costs just 25 cents to make.) That steep tab has put the drug’s lifesaving potential out of reach for some cancer patients, who have been forced into debt or simply stopped taking the drug. The price also helps fuel our ballooning insurance premiums. For decades, I’ve reported on outrageous health care costs in the U.S. and the burden they place on patients. I’ve revealed the tactics used by drug companies to drive sales and keep the price of their products high. Even with my experience, the cost of Revlimid stood out. When I started taking the drug, I’d look at the smooth, cylindrical capsule in my hand and consider the fact I was about to swallow something that costs about the same as a new iPhone. A month’s supply, which arrives in an ordinary, orange-tinged plastic bottle, is the same price as a new Nissan Versa. I wanted to know how this drug came to cost so much — and why the price keeps going up. The price of Revlimid has been hiked 26 times since it launched. Some of what happened was reported at the time. But no one has pieced together the full account of what the drugmaker Celgene did, how federal regulators failed to rein it in and what the story reveals about unrestrained drug pricing in America. What I discovered astonished even me. My journey started with an indefatigable New York City lawyer on a quest to give her dying husband a chance. Tiny and Terrifying Beth Wolmer’s story begins on a moon-splashed beach in the Cayman Islands in the winter of 1995. She and her husband, Ira, were holding hands as they walked in the sand, enjoying a rare break from a hectic life as parents to a 1-year-old daughter and demanding jobs as 30-something professionals in New York City. They had met through friends and clicked from the start. On Sunday mornings, they sat together for hours, sharing sections of the newspaper and eating bagels. They planned trips to Europe and outings to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Ira was an interventional cardiologist who followed his father into medicine. Beth was a lawyer at the high-powered firm Skadden Arps. “We had a great life,” Beth told me. “I specifically remember coming home on the bus and thinking: ‘My life is just perfect, perfect. I’m not going to change a thing.’” As they walked that night in the Caribbean, Ira felt a sharp pain in his cheekbone. The pain flared several more times during the trip, becoming so intense that it brought tears to his eyes. When he got home, Ira made an appointment to figure out what was wrong. Imaging tests revealed multiple myeloma. The prognosis was grim. The couple was told Ira had two years to live. Specialists recommended treatments that would only provide a brief reprieve. The couple searched for someone who could offer something more. That’s when they found Dr. Bart Barlogie in Little Rock, Arkansas. I’ve never been more scared of a spouse of a patient than I was of her. —Dr. David Siegel, who treated Ira Wolmer Barlogie had been recruited to the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences from the more prestigious MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston. In Texas, Barlogie had been frustrated by a medical culture that he viewed as too timid in its approach to multiple myeloma. He remembers working on a Sunday when a newly diagnosed patient was admitted to the hospital. With few options, Barlogie decided to put the patient on a taxing, four-drug chemotherapy cocktail used for lymphoma patients. It didn’t work. The patient died from a sepsis infection, a known complication of the treatment. The attending physician later admonished him, Barlogie said, saying, “Bart, we have to learn to treat myeloma gently.” Barlogie said he thought to himself, “Fuck you.” In Arkansas, Barlogie was in charge. He quickly developed a reputation as a practitioner willing to try anything to fight the fatal disease. Patients from around the world — including the actor Roy Scheider from the movie “Jaws” — flocked to his clinic. Beth and Ira heard Barlogie before they saw him. The cowboy boots he’d taken to donning since his time in Houston clacked down the linoleum hallway floors. A short, slight man, Barlogie had a booming voice with a German accent. He wore leather jackets and round, red-framed glasses on his bald head. When he strode into the exam room, he hugged Beth and Ira and told them they had come to the right place. Now retired, Barlogie recalls being struck by Beth’s intensity. He said she told him “you must do something” to help Ira. I met Barlogie at his home in Little Rock. We sat in his office, which is filled with photos of the red Ducati motorcycle he used to ride to work. An old license plate with the letters “MMCURED” sat on a shelf, reflecting his goal to find a cure for multiple myeloma. When Beth and Ira found him, Barlogie told me, he had been having some success with a novel approach that put patients through two stem cell transplants a few months apart, which he called a tandem stem cell transplant. With a transplant, a patient is bombarded with high-dose chemotherapy to kill the cancerous plasma cells. The patient is then infused with healthy stem cells that travel to the bone marrow. The intense chemotherapy can be grueling and poses a small risk of death. Ira underwent three transplants. Each time, he relapsed. By the fall of 1997, after two years of treatment, Ira’s thick black hair was gone. He was losing weight. Then he had a stroke. His kidneys failed and required dialysis. He developed pneumonia and had to be intubated

item.title: PlaceIt3D: Language-Guided Object Placement in Real 3D Scenes
item.summary:
We introduce the novel task of Language-Guided Object Placement in Real 3D
Scenes. Our model is given a 3D scene's point cloud, a 3D asset, and a textual
prompt broadly describing where the 3D asset should be placed. The task here is
to find a valid placement for the 3D asset that respects the prompt. Compared
with other language-guided localization tasks in 3D scenes such as grounding,
this task has specific challenges: it is ambiguous because it has multiple
valid solutions, and it requires reasoning about 3D geometric relationships and
free space. We inaugurate this task by proposing a new benchmark and evaluation
protocol. We also introduce a new dataset for training 3D LLMs on this task, as
well as the first method to serve as a non-trivial baseline. We believe that
this challenging task and our new benchmark could become part of the suite of
benchmarks used to evaluate and compare generalist 3D LLM models.

narrative_raw:
# Today in Tech: Monitoring Models, Managing Data, and Mamba's Evolution

Let's talk about what actually matters in today's batch of papers and announcements.

## Model Monitoring Without Ground Truth

First up, there's this "CBPE" method for estimating binary classifier performance without ground truth labels. This is a genuinely useful development. 

The problem they're solving is real: you deploy a model, but you don't know if it's still performing well because you don't have immediate access to the true labels. Traditional monitoring requires these labels, creating an annoying latency or making monitoring impossible.

What's interesting is they're moving beyond just accuracy estimation (which others have tackled) to estimate any metric defined from the confusion matrix - precision, recall, F1, etc. The approach treats confusion matrix elements as random variables and uses calibrated confidence scores to estimate their distributions.

The key insight: if your model is well-calibrated (its confidence scores actually correspond to probabilities of correctness), you can leverage this to estimate performance metrics without seeing the actual labels. They're also providing confidence intervals on these estimates, which is crucial for practical applications.

## Nao Labs: Data-Aware Code Editor

This YC startup is building what they're calling "Cursor for Data" - basically a specialized code editor for data work. The core idea is integrating the code editor directly with data warehouses and adding an AI copilot that actually understands your data schema.

What's potentially valuable here is the focus on data-specific workflows. Regular code-focused LLM tools like Cursor don't natively connect to data warehouses, so they're autocompleting SQL without knowing your actual schema. The Nao editor shows you code diffs alongside data diffs, so you can immediately see how your changes affect outputs.

I'm skeptical about their "fork of VS Code" approach rather than building extensions, but their integration of RAG with your data schema and codebase could be genuinely useful for data teams. The emphasis on data quality checks and lineage impact analysis addresses real pain points.

## PRE-Mamba: State Space Models for Event Cameras

This paper represents an interesting application of state space models (the tech behind Mamba) to a very specific domain: cleaning up noise from event cameras in rainy conditions.

Event cameras are these specialized sensors that capture changes in brightness at extremely high temporal resolution rather than full frames. They're great for high-dynamic-range scenes but get noisy in rain.

The technical innovation here is their "4D event cloud representation" with dual temporal scales and a "Multi-Scale State Space Model" that captures rain dynamics across different temporal and spatial scales. The computational efficiency is impressive - they're getting strong performance with only 0.26M parameters, which is tiny by modern standards.

This is part of a broader trend of state space models being applied to specialized domains beyond general text modeling.

## Elastic Reasoning: Scalable Chain of Thought

This paper addresses a practical problem with LLMs that use chain-of-thought reasoning: they can ramble on forever, consuming tokens and compute. When you have real-world constraints on inference time or token budgets, this becomes problematic.

Their solution, "Elastic Reasoning," explicitly separates reasoning into two phases - thinking and solution - with separate budgets. The clever part is their training approach, which teaches models to be robust to truncated thinking processes. They use a "budget-constrained rollout strategy" that trains the model to adapt when its thinking gets cut short.

What makes this particularly useful is that it generalizes to unseen budget constraints without additional training. And interestingly, they found that this approach produces more concise reasoning even in unconstrained settings - suggesting that forcing the model to be efficient actually improves its reasoning quality.

## Vision in Llama.cpp

The extract is incomplete, but the headline tells us that vision capabilities are now available in llama.cpp, which is significant for local deployment of multimodal models. Llama.cpp has been crucial for running LLMs on consumer hardware, and adding vision capabilities expands what's possible without cloud dependencies.

## ICon: Data Selection Through In-Context Contribution

This paper tackles the problem of selecting the most valuable data for instruction tuning LLMs. Traditional methods either use expensive gradient-based measures or rely on manually designed heuristics.

Their approach, "ICon," leverages in-context learning to measure sample contribution without computing gradients. The insight is that you can use the model's performance shifts under in-context learning as a proxy for how valuable a sample would be for fine-tuning.

The results are impressive: models trained on just 15% of ICon-selected data outperform models trained on complete datasets by 5.42 percentage points. This suggests there's a lot of low-value or even harmful data in standard instruction tuning datasets.

The analysis of what makes high-contribution samples is interesting too - they're diverse in task types and have appropriate difficulty levels, not just the hardest examples.

## The Thalidomide Derivative Revlimid: Pricing Ethics

This ProPublica piece tells the story of a cancer drug called Revlimid, a derivative of thalidomide that has become one of the best-selling pharmaceutical products ever with over $100 billion in sales.

The shocking part is the pricing: nearly $1,000 per pill, while it costs just 25 cents to manufacture. The journalist, who has multiple myeloma and takes the drug, notes that a month's supply costs about the same as a new Nissan Versa.

This isn't just abstract price gouging - the article mentions patients forced into debt or stopping treatment entirely because of the cost. The price has been hiked 26 times since launch, and the full story involves regulatory failures and exploitation of patent laws.

## PlaceIt3D: Placing Objects in 3D Scenes

This paper introduces a new task for 3D scene understanding: placing objects in real 3D scenes based on natural language instructions. Given a 3D scene point cloud, a 3D asset, and a text prompt (like "put the chair next to the sofa"), the model needs to find valid placements.

What makes this challenging is that it's ambiguous (multiple valid solutions exist) and requires reasoning about 3D geometric relationships and available space. The authors have created a benchmark, evaluation protocol, and a dataset for training 3D LLMs on this task.

This is part of the broader trend toward more sophisticated 3D understanding in AI systems, which will be crucial for robotics and AR/VR applications.
